Troubleshooting

Is my agent broken?

Almost always, no. Archie is built to stay quiet when there is nothing worth saying, and a quiet agent and a stopped agent look exactly the same from the outside. This page is the difference between the two: find the thing you saw, and it tells you which one it was.

Silence is a decision, and the decision is written down

Every time Archie reads an email or a text, it decides whether it is something you need to hear about. When the answer is no, it writes that down: who it was from, what it was about, and why it decided to leave it alone. So there is no such thing as an unexplained quiet morning. There is a quiet morning, and a record of it.

You can read that record yourself, and most of the answers below point you at it. In Archie, open your agent, go to the Email tab, and under Tell me about you will find Read and left alone: every email that arrived today and did not reach you, with the reason on each line. The Texts tab has the same list, under Which texts to watch.

What you saw, and what it means

Show

It said nothing at all

The most common reason to think an agent has died. Five of these six are Archie doing the thing you asked it to do.

What is happening

Archie asks two questions about every new email: did a human being write this, and does it want a personal reply from you. A note from your accountant saying “got it, thanks” passes the first and fails the second.

Which of those two has to be true before Archie tells you is a setting, and it starts on the strictest position, Only mail that needs a reply from me. So an email that is real but asks nothing of you is read and deliberately left alone.

How to check

In Archie, open your agent, go to the Email tab, and look under Tell me about for the list called Read and left alone. If your email is on it, this is what happened, and the line will say which of the two reasons it was.

What to do about it

If you would rather hear about that email, widen the setting: on the same Tell me about panel, pick Anything a real person sent me. From then on Archie tells you about anything a human typed, whether or not it wants an answer back.

This does not cost more. Both judgments are already made in the same read, so widening the setting changes how many messages you get and not what you spend on your AI account.

What is happening

Archie is reading your inbox, but it does not yet know where to put the news. It learns that from you: the conversation you message it in first becomes the conversation it answers in.

What to do about it

Open the place you want to hear from your agent, which is the chat inside Archie or whichever chat app you connected, and send it one message. Anything at all. Inbox news arrives there from then on.

What is happening

When your agent has been off for more than an hour and a pile has built up, it does not fire twelve separate messages at you. It reads the pile and sends one numbered list of what is in it.

Nothing is dropped. Every line on that list is a message it is holding for you, and the list also counts the ones that needed nothing, so the numbers add back up to what arrived.

What to do about it

Answer with the number. Sending “3” opens the third one properly and offers to write the reply. Archie keeps the list for a day, so a list from this morning still works this evening.

What is happening

Writing a draft is the part that costs money on your AI account, so there is a ceiling on how many Archie will write per hour. You set the number. When it reaches the ceiling it stops writing drafts and waits for the hour to turn over.

What to do about it

The number is on the Email tab, under How often, and how many. Raising it means more drafts per hour and a higher bill on your AI account, so it is a spending decision rather than a performance one. That is why it is a number you type instead of a switch we picked for you.

What is happening

Your agent runs on your own computer rather than on ours, and it reads your inbox from there. While that computer is asleep, shut down, or has Archie closed, nothing is being read. Nothing is lost either: the moment it starts again, Archie catches up on everything that arrived while it was off.

This is the trade that makes the rest of Archie true. Your mail is read on a computer you own, so there is no server of ours holding it.

What to do about it

Go and look at the computer running Archie. It needs three things: powered on and awake, connected to the internet, and Archie itself open. Closing the window is not the same as quitting the app; if you quit it, open it again and it picks up on its own with nothing for you to set up a second time.

If you want it working while you are out, that computer has to stay awake. On a Mac, open System Settings, then Battery, and turn off sleep while plugged into power. A wired cable from your router beats Wi-Fi here, because every Wi-Fi drop is time your agent spends stopped.

What is happening

Two settings can stop an email reaching you, and they work differently. Never tell me about drops it before Archie reads it at all, on a word you typed. Tell me about drops it after reading, on the judgment Archie made.

The first is the one worth checking for accidents. A rule on the word “invoice” is doing exactly what you asked when it hides your plumber’s invoice too.

What to do about it

On the Email tab, read the list under Never tell me about and take out anything broader than you meant. Then, if the sender was a real person, move Tell me about one position wider to Anything a real person sent me.

There is a third option for one particular sender you never want missed. Under When a reply is wanted, the setting Always write a reply, even when it looks like none is needed lets you name people by email address. Archie stops judging their mail and always brings it to you.

It did something I did not expect

Things Archie does on purpose that read, the first time, like a mistake.

What is happening

Archie never sends an email or a text on its own. Every draft is a proposal: a text goes nowhere until you press Send, and an email goes nowhere until you send it or set a time for it yourself. There is no setting that turns this off, and that is deliberate: an assistant that answers your clients unsupervised is a different and much worse product.

What to do about it

Read the draft, change anything you want with Edit, and press Send. If it is wrong, tell your agent what to fix in your own words and it will write it again.

What is happening

Reading your mailbox and sending from it are two separate permissions, granted at different moments. It is normal to have given the first and not the second, and it looks like a dead button rather than a missing permission.

What to do about it

In Archie, open the Connections tab. Under Email, calendar, files, find the account and press Reconnect. Google or Microsoft will show you a list of permissions to approve: tick the one about sending mail. The Send button works from then on, including on drafts you already have waiting.

An iCloud, Fastmail, Yahoo, AOL, Zoho Mail or GMX account has no permission list. Press Reconnect, paste the app password again, and Archie tries the outgoing mail server with it. Sending stays off until that server accepts the password; if it keeps refusing, make a new app password on the provider’s site and reconnect with that one.

What is happening

A draft waits until you look at it, and while it waits Archie keeps watching that conversation. If you answer from your phone, or the other person writes again, Archie pulls the stale draft back rather than letting you send an answer to a conversation that has moved on.

The gap is the few minutes between a draft being written and the next check, so a draft you happen to see right after answering elsewhere can still be sitting there.

What to do about it

Nothing. Dismiss it, or leave it: it would have been withdrawn on its own.

What is happening

A drafted reply goes out under your name, not your agent’s, so it is written to match the email it is answering rather than the personality you picked. The personality governs how your agent talks to you.

What to do about it

If the drafts are consistently not how you write, say so to your agent in chat, in plain words: “when you draft my email, keep it to two sentences and never open with I hope this finds you well.” It keeps that and applies it to the next one.

An account has stopped working

Nothing you did. A sign-in lapses, a password changes, an administrator withdraws access, and the reading stops.

What is happening

The permission you gave Archie has stopped working. That happens on its own: Google or Microsoft withdrew it, or you changed your password, or an administrator at your company revoked access. Archie keeps trying every half minute and keeps being turned away, so the mail is still in your inbox and none of it is reaching you.

How to check

In Archie, open the Connections tab and look at the account under Email, calendar, files. An account that has stopped working says Not opening and how long it has been that way, with the reason underneath it in Google’s or Microsoft’s own words.

Worth knowing what that badge is and is not. The other badges on that row say what you granted, which is still true of an account that has stopped working, so a row of them is not proof of anything. Not opening is the only one that reports whether the last read actually succeeded, and it is the one to read.

What to do about it

Press Reconnect on that row and sign in again, approving the permissions. If there is no Reconnect button, remove the account and add it back. Either way is safe at any time and loses nothing: your settings, your drafts and your agent’s memory are untouched by it, and the mail that piled up while the account was out is read as soon as it opens again.

For an iCloud, Fastmail, Yahoo, AOL, Zoho Mail or GMX account, Reconnect asks for the app password again. If you changed the password on the account itself, make a new app password first: Apple, for one, cancels every app-specific password the moment the Apple ID password changes, and the old one will keep being turned away.

What is happening

An add-on that needs an account it can no longer reach will tell you it cannot do the job, without naming the account as the reason. Usually this is the same expired permission as the answer above, seen from the other end.

What to do about it

Ask your agent straight out: “why couldn’t you do that?” It can read its own error and will usually name the connection. Then reconnect that one on the Connections tab.

Text messages

Texts have two limits that email does not, and both of them look like faults.

What is happening

Text watching reads the Messages app on a Mac. It needs Archie running on that Mac, signed in to the same Apple account your texts arrive on, and given permission to read that app’s files. On Windows there is no equivalent for it to read, so the feature is Mac only.

What to do about it

In Archie, open the Texts tab. It names whichever of those is missing and gives you the button that fixes it. If it is the permission, macOS asks for it once and then remembers.

What is happening

On an agent shared by more than one person, text watching serves the owner only. A mailbox belongs to an account, so a shared agent can hold several and give each person their own. There is one Messages app per Mac and it belongs to whoever is signed into it, so a second person asking about texts would be asking to read the owner’s.

What to do about it

Nothing changes this on a shared agent, by design. If you want your own texts watched, that means your own agent on your own Mac.

Nothing in that category. Press Everything to see the rest.

If none of that is it

Then it is ours, and we would rather have the record than a description of it. Your agent keeps a technical log of what it did, and sending it saves a round of guessing.

  1. In Archie, open your agent and click Activity at the bottom of the screen.
  2. Press Export to save the whole log to a file.
  3. Email it to questions@otianai.com, with roughly when the thing happened and who the message was from.

That log holds what your agent read and what it decided. It does not carry the contents of your emails or your texts.
